# How to Run Your First Viral ChatGPT Trend Prompt From Start to Finish

> **In short:** You can copy a trend prompt, paste it into ChatGPT, fill in your own details, and decide whether the answer is worth keeping. No tool can guarantee a post goes viral, so check every fact and never share private information.

Trend prompts are short instructions that many people copy and personalize, such as "write a funny caption about my week" or "describe my morning routine as a movie trailer." By the end of this guide, you will have run one complete prompt from start to finish, from finding it to deciding whether to keep the result. It is written for complete beginners, so every step explains what to look for.

## Before you start

- **A ChatGPT account.** You can use the ChatGPT website or the mobile app. Some features may need a paid plan, so check your account settings if something is locked.
- **A notes app on your phone or computer.** You will use it to save a safe copy of the prompt and your final draft.
- **About 20 minutes and an open mind.** Expect to run the prompt two or three times before you like the result.

## Step 1 — Find a trend prompt and copy it

Trend prompts are often shared in social media posts, captions, comments, blog articles with a list of prompt ideas, or newsletters. If you are not sure where to look, try searching a phrase like "ChatGPT trend prompts" in a search engine, and open a result from a site you already trust. You can also check the posts of creators you already follow.

When you find a prompt you like, press and hold the text until a selection box appears, then drag the handles to cover the whole prompt. Tap the "Copy" option that appears, or use the copy shortcut on a computer. Paste the text into your notes app so you have a safe copy to edit.

Now read the whole prompt and look for **square brackets**. These are the symbols [like this]. They are placeholders, which means spots that are waiting for your own details. Also look for blanks or words such as "your job" or "your city." Those are the spots you will personalize in Step 3. If the prompt asks you to upload a photo of another person, skip it unless that person has agreed.

You'll know it worked when the full prompt sits in your notes app and you can point to at least one bracket or blank that needs your details.

## Step 2 — Open a new chat and paste the prompt

Open ChatGPT and start a new chat. On the website or app, this is usually a button that looks like a pencil on a page or a plus sign. Once the new chat opens, you should see an empty area with a message box at the bottom of the screen. Tap inside that box so a blinking cursor appears.

Now paste your copied prompt. Press and hold inside the message box and choose the paste option, or use the paste shortcut on a computer. The full text should appear in the message box. Nothing has been sent yet, so you can still edit it. Leave the text as it is for now, because your personal details come next.

If you do not see a message box, look for a text field near the bottom of the screen. Layouts differ between phones, tablets and computers, so take a moment to scan the screen before you give up.

💬 Example: "Write a short, funny caption for a photo of [your pet] doing [everyday activity]."

You'll know it worked when your pasted text is visible in the message box and ready for editing.

## Step 3 — Swap in your own details

Now replace each bracket and blank you found in Step 1 with your own information. Keep the sentence structure, but change the words that describe you. Remove the square brackets themselves, so the sentence reads naturally. Use only details you are comfortable sharing, such as a hobby, a job title or a general city. Leave out your home address, phone number, passwords, and anything about other people that they have not agreed to share.

Tap inside the message box and edit the text. If a bracket says [your job], type your real job or a general version, such as "nurse," "teacher" or "warehouse worker." Keep your edits short so the prompt still reads clearly. If editing feels awkward, select the words you want to change and type over them. If you accidentally delete the whole prompt, paste the copy from your notes app again.

💬 Example: "Rewrite this for my life: I'm a [job title] in [your city] who loves [hobby]."

You'll know it worked when the prompt reads like a sentence about you and no square brackets remain.

## Step 4 — Send it and read the first answer

Send your message. On most screens, the send button is a small arrow or paper-plane icon at the right edge of the message box. Your message will appear in the chat, and ChatGPT's answer will appear below it, often word by word. Wait until the answer stops moving before you judge it.

Read it once for the big picture. If it misses the point, do not start over. Send a follow-up message that asks for one specific change. ChatGPT can adjust a draft quickly, but it cannot know your real life unless you tell it, and it cannot check today's news on its own unless the tool you are using has that feature.

If nothing happens after you send, check your internet connection and try again. If you see a message about usage limits, you may need to wait a while or check your plan.

💬 Example: "Make this shorter, keep the humor, and remove any joke about [topic you dislike]."

You'll know it worked when a new answer appears under your last message and it reflects the change you asked for.

## Step 5 — Judge whether the result is worth keeping

This step matters most. Read the answer slowly and ask yourself four questions. Does it sound like you, or like a stranger? Does it make any claim about a real person, company or fact? Would you feel comfortable if a stranger read it? Is it actually funny, useful or interesting to you?

If a fact or claim looks questionable, check it with a trusted source before you use it. ChatGPT can write confident sentences that are simply incorrect, so treat its output as a draft. You can ask it to list the claims you should verify, then check each one yourself.

If the result fails any of the four checks, that is useful information. It tells you exactly what to change in your next message.

💬 Example: "List every factual claim in your last answer so I can check each one before I post it."

You'll know it worked when you have a short list of claims to verify, or you feel confident the draft passes all four questions.

## Step 6 — Save your favorite version

When you have a result you like, copy it into your notes app and label it with today's date and the name of the prompt. That way you can find it later. Your chat history may also keep the conversation, usually in a sidebar or menu, so you can return to it.

Before you post anything, reread the final version once more. Remove any detail you do not want public. If you plan to share a photo, check that it shows nothing private, such as a street sign, a license plate or a document.

If you cannot find your old chat, rely on your notes copy. That copy is your safest backup.

💬 Example: "Give me the final version in plain text with no headings so I can paste it into my notes."

You'll know it worked when your finished draft is saved outside the chat and you have reread it once before sharing.

## Common mistakes

- **Posting without checking.** A trend prompt can produce a claim that sounds right but is wrong. The fix is to run Step 5 every time and verify any fact before it goes public.
- **Sharing private details.** Your full name, address or a photo of someone else can end up online. The fix is to use general details and ask people before you include them.
- **Expecting a guaranteed hit.** ChatGPT can write a good draft, but no tool can promise that a post will catch attention. Many people find that personal, honest posts feel more engaging, though results vary. The fix is to treat each result as one draft among many and enjoy the process.

## What this means for you

- **In everyday life:** You can use trend prompts to write a birthday card message, a funny family group caption or a quick travel plan, then adjust the result until it feels like you.
- **For your business or work:** A trend prompt can give you a starting point for a short social post or a slogan idea. Always check any claim, and keep your own brand voice in the final version.
- **If you're just getting started:** Begin with a low-stakes prompt for a private message to a friend, and practice Steps 4 and 5 before you try anything public.

## Try it now

Copy one trend prompt into your notes app, replace one square bracket with a detail about yourself, and send it to ChatGPT. Read the answer and ask yourself the four questions from Step 5. You can finish this first run in about two minutes.
